questions.q: What is software testing, in one sentence?
options: Evaluating a program against expectations to find defects and provide information about quality

questions.q: Why can't you test without expected results?
options: Without knowing the correct behavior you can't tell a defect from a feature; you've only observed output

questions.q: What does 'testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects' imply?
options: Passing tests can't prove a program is bug-free

questions.q: Why is a test that lives only in your head not a test?
options: It isn't repeatable or reviewable by anyone else

questions.q: What is the difference between a test scenario and a test case?
options: A scenario is a high-level thing to test; a case has precise inputs, steps and expected results
questions.explain: Scenario, case and step differ in size and precision.

questions.q: What does traceability link?
options: Tests back to the requirements they verify
questions.explain: It shows what's covered and what isn't.

questions.q: What should a good test case's expected result be?
options: Specific and observable, so pass/fail is unambiguous

questions.q: What belongs in test data design?
options: Representative, boundary and invalid values, kept under control and documented
questions.explain: Data is part of the test.

questions.q: Which are the test levels from smallest to largest?
questions.explain: Levels describe how much of the system is under test.

questions.q: Which is a non-functional test type?
questions.explain: Functional checks what; non-functional checks how well.

questions.q: What does regression testing check?
options: That previously working behavior still works after a change

questions.q: Why say precisely 'which tests at which level'?
options: 'We tested it' hides what wasn't tested

questions.q: What must a C/C++ bug report include beyond steps?
options: Build flags, sanitizer output, version and the exact input bytes

questions.q: Which is the best bug title?
What's the typical defect lifecycle order?
A developer says 'cannot reproduce'. What helps?
options: A minimal reproducer with exact environment and inputs

questions.q: When is exploratory testing valuable?
options: To find unexpected problems by learning and testing at once, guided by a charter

questions.q: Why note what you did during exploratory sessions?
options: So findings can be reproduced and coverage understood

questions.q: Which task suits manual testing?
options: Usability and one-off investigation that isn't worth automating

questions.q: What's a smoke test?
options: A quick check that the build's basic functions work before deeper testing

questions.q: Why enable -Wall -Wextra?
options: Warnings find bugs at compile time for free

questions.q: What does -g do?
options: Adds debug symbols so debuggers and sanitizers show source lines

questions.q: What does -Werror do?
options: Treats warnings as errors so they can't be ignored

questions.q: Why record compiler and version in a bug report?
options: Behavior and diagnostics differ across compilers and versions

questions.q: What does TEST(Suite, Name) do?
options: Registers a test case automatically with GoogleTest

questions.q: What's the difference between EXPECT_EQ and ASSERT_EQ?
options: EXPECT_* records a failure and continues; ASSERT_* stops the current test
questions.explain: Use ASSERT when continuing is meaningless.

questions.q: Why add a descriptive failure message?
options: So a failure is understandable without opening the source

questions.q: What do fixtures share?
options: Setup and teardown for related tests via TEST_F

questions.q: When is Unity a good choice?
options: Tiny embedded targets: it is small with zero dependencies

questions.q: What does CMocka offer that Unity lacks out of the box?
How do you test C code with GoogleTest?
options: Wrap the C headers in extern "C" and compile tests as C++

questions.q: Why do plain C tests need a runner?
options: C has no automatic test registration; tests are listed explicitly or via macros

questions.q: What does ctest do?
options: Runs the tests registered with CMake and reports each separately

questions.q: Why use the same tests in debug, release and sanitizer builds?
What does `ctest --output-on-failure` do?
options: Shows test output only for failing tests

questions.q: How should a growing suite be organized?
Why pair a manual test plan with an automated suite?
options: The plan says what to verify and why; automation locks in what's cheap to rerun

questions.q: What should a test plan include?
options: Scope, approach, risks, cases, environment and exit criteria

questions.q: What's the right candidate for automation?
How do you keep the plan useful?
options: Link cases to requirements and update as the product changes

questions.q: What do parameterized tests (TEST_P) avoid?
options: Copy-pasting the same test logic for many inputs

questions.q: When do SetUpTestSuite/TearDownTestSuite run?
options: Once per suite rather than per test, e.g. for expensive shared setup

questions.q: What do typed tests verify?
How do you make failure messages useful?
options: Stream context with << or use matchers with descriptive output

questions.q: What does a mock let you assert?
options: The interaction itself: whether a call happened, with what args, in what order

questions.q: What makes a collaborator mockable in C++?
Why do mocks make tests faster and more reliable?
options: They remove slow, non-deterministic dependencies like networks
questions.explain: Unit tests fail for one reason.

questions.q: What is over-mocking?
options: Mocking so much that tests check implementation details instead of behavior

questions.q: How do you control a mocked C function's return?
options: will_return() queues values that mock() returns

questions.q: What does expect_value / check_expected do?
options: Verifies the arguments passed to the mocked function

questions.q: Why use linker wrapping (--wrap) for mocking C?
options: It substitutes functions you don't own without changing source

questions.q: What does CMocka's test_malloc detect?
options: Leaks and heap corruption in code under test

questions.q: What does AddressSanitizer detect?
options: Heap/stack buffer overflows, use-after-free and leaks

questions.q: Why can a program with a buffer overflow still pass tests?
options: The write may hit unused memory and the answer is right until the layout shifts

questions.q: How does valgrind differ from ASan?
options: It runs the unmodified binary under emulation: slower, no recompile

questions.q: What does LeakSanitizer report?
options: Heap allocations never freed at exit

questions.q: Why can UB pass at -O0 and fail at -O2?
options: The optimizer may assume UB never happens and transform the code

questions.q: Which is undefined behavior?
What does UBSan do?
options: Instruments code to report UB like overflow and invalid shifts at runtime

questions.q: Why run UBSan in tests?
options: UB bugs are invisible to ordinary assertions

questions.q: What does line coverage tell you?
options: Which lines executed during tests, not whether assertions were meaningful

questions.q: Why can 100% line coverage hide untested logic?
options: A line with multiple conditions can run without exercising every outcome
questions.explain: Use branch coverage and strong assertions.

questions.q: Which flag enables gcov instrumentation?
Branch coverage measures...
options: Whether each decision's true and false outcomes were taken

questions.q: What is a seam?
options: A place where behavior can be substituted for testing
questions.explain: Code lacking seams is untestable as written.

questions.q: Which double returns canned answers?
What's a fake?
options: A working but simplified implementation, like an in-memory filesystem

questions.q: How do you test code reading a register at 0x40?
options: Abstract the register access behind an interface or function you can replace

questions.q: Why prefer targets with PUBLIC/PRIVATE properties over global variables?
What does add_test register?
options: A test for ctest to run, reported individually

questions.q: How do you run a sanitizer build alongside normal one?
options: Separate build directories or presets with different flags

questions.q: What does `ctest -R name` do?
options: Runs tests whose names match the regex

questions.q: How does static analysis differ from dynamic testing?
options: It reasons about source paths without running them

questions.q: Why do analyzers get a bad reputation?

questions.q: Which tool is a C/C++ static analyzer/linter?
How should findings be triaged?
options: Fix real bugs, suppress with justification and tune noisy checks

questions.q: What does the instrumented suite combine?
options: Sanitizers, coverage and static analysis on one test suite

questions.q: Why build each configuration separately?
options: Sanitizers and coverage change codegen and shouldn't mix

questions.q: What is the purpose of coverage reports in CI?
options: Spot untested code and watch trends, not as a goal by itself

questions.q: What should fail the CI job?
options: Failing tests, sanitizer reports and static-analysis errors

questions.q: What is a big-bang integration approach's weakness?
options: Failures are hard to localize because everything is integrated at once

questions.q: What does top-down integration use for missing lower modules?
What does integration testing verify?
What's a contract test?
options: Verifies both sides of an interface agree on its behavior

questions.q: Why run some tests on the real target?
options: Compiler, word size and hardware behavior can differ from the host

questions.q: What is a common technique for on-target results?

questions.q: What limits embedded tests?

questions.q: What does a host-based test with a hardware abstraction layer give you?
options: Fast feedback on logic without the device

questions.q: What is HIL testing?
options: Running real firmware against simulated or real hardware inputs under automation

questions.q: What makes HIL tests slow and costly?
options: Physical devices, setup and limited parallelism

questions.q: Which belongs in HIL rather than host tests?
What helps HIL reliability?

questions.q: What does fuzzing do?
options: Feeds many generated/mutated inputs to find crashes and sanitizer errors
questions.explain: Finds what you didn't think of.

questions.q: Why combine fuzzing with sanitizers?
options: Silent memory errors become visible failures

questions.q: What is a corpus?
options: A set of interesting inputs that guide and persist fuzzing progress

questions.q: What should you do with a fuzzer crash?
options: Minimize it into a regression test

questions.q: What is a property-based test?
options: It checks an invariant over many generated inputs instead of fixed examples

questions.q: What does shrinking do?
options: Reduces a failing input to a minimal counterexample

questions.q: Which is a good property for sort()?
options: Output is ordered and a permutation of the input

questions.q: When do examples still matter?
options: For documenting key cases and regressions

questions.q: What should a CI pipeline for C/C++ tests include?
options: Build matrix, tests, sanitizers, coverage and static analysis

questions.q: Why cache dependencies and build outputs in CI?
options: To cut run time and keep feedback fast

questions.q: Why run sanitizer builds as separate jobs?
options: They need different flags and are slower

questions.q: What's a flaky test's effect on CI?
options: It erodes trust and teaches people to ignore failures

questions.q: Why benchmark in release builds?
options: Debug builds have different performance characteristics

questions.q: What can the optimizer do to a benchmark?
options: Eliminate work whose result is unused, so use sinks or DoNotOptimize

questions.q: Why run benchmarks multiple times?

questions.q: What's a performance regression test?

questions.q: Which tool finds data races?
Why are concurrency bugs hard to test?

questions.q: What helps reproduce a race?

questions.q: Which is a deadlock cause?

options: Substituting behavior at a point without editing the code there

questions.q: What's the first step before refactoring untested code?

questions.q: What does the pipeline combine?
options: Sanitizers, coverage and fuzzing in CI

questions.q: What should happen to a new fuzz crash?

questions.q: What should fail the pipeline?
options: Test failures, sanitizer findings and new crashes

questions.q: Why organize tests by layers (unit, integration, system)?
options: So fast tests run often and slow tests run where needed

questions.q: What does test isolation require?

questions.q: Why share fixtures and helpers in a common library?
options: To reduce duplication and keep tests consistent

questions.q: What makes large suites slow?
options: Too many integration tests and expensive setup; parallelize and prune

questions.q: What do standards like DO-178C or ISO 26262 demand of testing?

questions.q: Why is requirement-to-test traceability central?
options: Auditors must see each requirement verified

questions.q: What does MC/DC coverage check?

questions.q: Does passing tests alone satisfy a safety standard?

questions.q: What is requirements-based testing?

questions.q: What does a traceability matrix show?

questions.q: What should a testable requirement be?
What happens when a requirement changes?
How does formal verification differ from testing?
options: It proves properties over all inputs rather than sampling some

questions.q: What can bounded model checking do?
options: Explore all executions up to a bound to find violations

questions.q: What is a limitation of formal methods?
options: They need precise specifications and effort, and verify only the model

questions.q: What is an assertion's role in verification?
options: States a property tools can check

questions.q: What does certification evidence include?
options: Plans, traceability, test results, coverage reports and reviews

questions.q: Why must reports be reproducible?
options: A reviewer must be able to regenerate results from the same inputs

questions.q: What makes a test report credible?
options: Exact versions, configuration, raw results and unexplained failures investigated

questions.q: What is test independence?
options: Someone other than the author verifies critical work

questions.q: What is cross-compilation?
options: Building on one architecture for another

questions.q: How can you run target binaries on the host?
options: With an emulator such as QEMU user mode

questions.q: Why still test on real hardware?

questions.q: What is a quality gate?

questions.q: How should assertion macros report failures?
What does the capstone integrate?
options: Unit, integration, sanitizers, coverage, fuzzing, CI and reporting

options: Reproducible, automated, fast and maintainable with clear gates

questions.q: How do you prove the infrastructure works?

questions.q: What should be documented for the team?

questions.q: A manager asks: 'Can you guarantee the release has no bugs if all tests pass?' What's the accurate answer?
options: No: testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence

questions.q: A valid age range is 18 to 65. Which inputs best expose off-by-one bugs?
Test inputs 20, 30 and 40 are all valid ages. What does equivalence partitioning say?

options: Steps, exact input, environment/build flags and sanitizer output to reproduce it

options: Real networks are slow and non-deterministic; a mock isolates the unit and lets you assert on interactions

questions.q: Code reads a register at fixed address 0x40 and can't be unit tested. What's the fix?
options: Introduce a seam: put register access behind an interface you can fake or stub

questions.q: Which pairing is right: stub, mock, fake?
options: Stub returns canned answers, mock verifies interactions, fake is a simplified working implementation

questions.q: A parser crashes on one malformed packet found by a fuzzer. What's the right follow-up?
options: Minimize the input and add it as a regression test with the fix

questions.q: Which property fits property-based testing of sort()?
options: Output is ordered and a permutation of the input
questions.explain: Check invariants over many generated inputs.

questions.q: A race appears once in 1000 runs. Which tool helps?
You must change untested legacy code. What first?
options: Write characterization tests capturing current behavior, creating seams as needed

questions.q: Which is the best pipeline order for C/C++ test CI?
options: Fast checks first (build, unit tests), then sanitizers, coverage, static analysis and longer fuzzing

questions.q: What does a requirements traceability matrix reveal?
options: Which requirements have tests and which don't

questions.q: A team sets a 90% coverage gate and tests start asserting nothing. What's the lesson?
options: Metrics become targets and get gamed; pair coverage with assertion quality (e.g. mutation testing)

questions.q: When should you write an in-house test framework?
options: When constraints (tiny targets, certification) rule out existing ones, accepting the maintenance cost

challenges.title: Boundary value analysis
challenges.prompt: Write boundary_values(lo, hi) returning the inputs to test for a valid range [lo, hi]: just below, on and just above each boundary, plus a nominal middle value. Then run them through valid_age (18 to 65).
challenges.starter:
def boundary_values(lo, hi):
    # return [lo-1, lo, lo+1, a nominal middle value, hi-1, hi, hi+1]
    return []

def valid_age(n):
    return 18 <= n <= 65

cases = boundary_values(18, 65)
print(cases)
print([valid_age(n) for n in cases])
challenges.expected:
[17, 18, 19, 41, 64, 65, 66]
[False, True, True, True, True, True, False]
challenges.solution:
def boundary_values(lo, hi):
    """Boundary value analysis for a valid range [lo, hi]:
    just below, on and just above each boundary, plus a nominal value."""
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    return [lo - 1, lo, lo + 1, mid, hi - 1, hi, hi + 1]

def valid_age(n):
    return 18 <= n <= 65

cases = boundary_values(18, 65)
print(cases)
print([valid_age(n) for n in cases])
challenges.explain: Bugs cluster at boundaries (off-by-one: < versus <=). Testing both sides of each edge detects them with just seven cases instead of the whole range. Verified by running the solution.

challenges.title: Mutation score
challenges.prompt: Implement mutation_report(ages): check that the suite passes on the original is_adult, then report which mutants it kills (the suite fails on them) and which survive. Compare a weak suite that only tests age 40 with a strong suite that tests 17, 18 and 40.
challenges.expected:
weak suite    score 1/4  survived: ['boundary >= to >', 'threshold 18 to 21', 'always true']
strong suite  score 4/4  survived: []
challenges.explain: The weak suite kills only the 'negated' mutant yet still passes on the original, much like a high-coverage suite with weak assertions. Boundary tests (17 and 18) kill all four. Verified by running the solution.
